comparison: Both strongly support the PCNA-dependent recruitment and function of Srs2 in checkpoint downregulation. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of genetic suppression (C28-C33), checkpoint assays (C37, C41), and chromatin fractionation data (C42-C43). Peer reviewers explicitly affirm these findings as 'well supported' and 'convincing evidence.' High agreement on core genetic and biochemical evidence.

Both support the temporal relationship between Mec1 activation and Srs2 sumoylation, and the genetic requirement for Mec1 but not Rad53. OpenEval highlights the sequential dependency (PCNA binding → sumoylation → RPA antagonism). Peer reviewers accept these findings without challenge, noting the kinetic analysis and Mec1 dependence as convincing. Strong concordance.

Both support the parallel pathway model involving Srs2 and Slx4-Rtt107. OpenEval emphasizes additive genetic interactions (C46, C49, C50) across multiple assays. Peer reviewers accept the parallel pathway interpretation, noting that genetic data with slx4RIM support this notion. Complete agreement on the buffering/redundancy model.

Both support the finding that Mec1 kinase activity is required for Srs2 sumoylation, but the S1964 phosphorylation site specifically is not. OpenEval notes consistency between negative results across multiple backgrounds (C63-C65) and biochemical data (C66). Peer reviewers accept these findings, noting the distinction between Mec1 requirement and S1964 involvement. Strong agreement.

Perfect overlap on claims C68-C69. Both support the negative results for Rfa1-S178 and rfa2 mutants. OpenEval notes the differential effects between rfa1 and rfa2 phosphorylation sites suggest complex RPA regulation. Peer reviewers accept these findings without challenge as part of exploring mechanistic details. Complete concordance.

Both address the spatial selectivity model (C97-C98) but with different levels of confidence. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED but notes the model 'remains somewhat speculative as direct evidence for differential Srs2 activity at different ssDNA regions is not provided.' Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with editor explicitly noting 'direct experimental evidence for this is currently lacking.' Agreement that model is plausible but not directly demonstrated.

Substantial overlap on foundational observations (C22, C27, C34-C36, C39-C40) regarding mutual suppression between rfa1-zm2 and srs2 mutants. OpenEval includes these as part of broader model support. Peer reviewers accept these as established context for mechanistic studies. Both treat as well-supported foundational data.

Overlap on claims C1-C2, C13-C14, C19-C20 regarding prior work on Srs2's role in RPA removal and checkpoint downregulation. OpenEval includes these in model integration. Peer reviewers treat these as established findings from prior work that provide context. Both accept as foundational background.

Both address protein characterization, specifically that mutant protein levels are unchanged (C21). OpenEval notes this is important for interpreting functional assays. Peer reviewer explicitly notes this 'alleviates some concern about the use of deletion mutants compared to point mutations.' Strong agreement on validation of protein stability.

Limited overlap on chromatin fractionation data (C42-C43). OpenEval includes this as part of broader support for PCNA-dependent mechanism. Peer reviewers accept this data as supporting the RPA removal model without specific critique. Both treat as supporting evidence.

Strong overlap on PCNA loading requirements and ssDNA structures (C70-C72, C100-C102). OpenEval rates background information as SUPPORTED and notes it provides context for spatial selectivity model. Peer reviewers include this in their UNCERTAIN evaluation of the spatial model, noting the model is reasonable but lacks direct evidence. Agreement on background accuracy, but different emphasis on model support.
